newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Bruton says hopes for fresh IRA ceasefire. [corrected 18:55 gmt]
newsitem.headline: Bruton says hopes for fresh IRA ceasefire. [corrected 18:55 gmt]

text.p: Irish Prime Minister John Bruton said on Friday he hoped the Irish Republican Army was concluding an internal debate to end its policy of violence and agree a new ceasefire in Northern Ireland.
"They have gone through extensive internal debates with a view to changing their policy," Bruton told reporters before holding talks with Austrian Chancellor Franz Vranitzky.
"I hope that this debate is coming to a conclusion and that we will be able to have a ceasefire that on this occasion will hold in all circumstances," he added.
Bruton, whose country holds the presidency of the European Union, is on a swing through European capitals ahead of an EU summit in Ireland next month.
He declined to put any time-scale on a possible fresh truce. (Corrects by deleting reference to Bruton declining to comment on Londonderry car bomb.)
"I am not making any predictions as to when this will happen," he said.

Bruton was speaking a day after the leader of Northern Ireland's moderate nationalist Social Democratic and Labour Party, John Hume, said he believed the IRA was ready to renew the ceasefire it abandoned in February if Britain agreed to proposals he put forward.
Media reports said Hume had had urged Britain to set a rigid timetable for the all-party peace talks on the future of Northern Ireland.
In exchange, the IRA would call a new truce so that Sinn Fein, the IRA's political wing, could be granted a seat at the talks table.
Britain and Ireland have said Sinn Fein will not be allowed into talks until the IRA declares a full ceasefire.
"I think there is a recognition within the Irish Republican Army that the tactics of violence are a failure," Bruton said.

The Londonderry car bomb, which was defused before it could explode, was planted by Irish Continuity Army Council guerrillas, said to have broken away from the IRA 10 years ago in protest at a peace strategy advocated by Sinn Fein.
While security analysts said the emergence of the group presented fresh risks to Northern Ireland's fragile peace process, Hume was confident the IRA was willing to call a new truce.
"I will put my head on the line for this. I am absolutely convinced now we can achieve an absolutely genuine, unequivocal restoration (of the ceasefire)," Hume told the BBC.
Sinn Fein says it wants an unconditional seat at the talks if the IRA does adopt a new truce in its war to end British rule of Northern Ireland.
